1:1: This is the title of the book. Here vision is used in the general sense of a message from the Lord, rather than to indicate how Obadiah received that message. Vision here is a metaphor for the way that God gives knowledge to people.
Some English translations call the prophet Abdias, but Obadiah is the form of his name most commonly used in English.
This is the name of God that he revealed to his people in the Old Testament.
People are being described here by the name of something closely associated with them, Edom, the land that they live in.
This phrase is used to tell people to get ready, in this case to attack Edom.
This is an idiom that means to violently oppose another person or nation.
Here, her refers to the land of Edom, which, again, stands for the people of Edom.
1:2: This alerts the people of Edom to pay special attention to what follows.
קָטֹן נְתַתִּיךָ בַּגּוֹיִם בָּזוּי אַתָּה מְאֹד
These two phrases mean similar things and are used together to emphasize that Edom will lose its important status.
Something insignificant is spoken of as if it were small in size and could easily be overlooked.
1:3: Here, pride is spoken of as though it were a person who could deceive someone.
Here, heart is used to refer to a person’s thoughts and feelings.
This means a place that is protected because it is surrounded by rocks.
Here, the heart is used to refer to a person’s thoughts and feelings.
This rhetorical question expresses how proud the Edomites were and how safe they felt.
1:4: אִם־תַּגְבִּיהַּ כַּנֶּשֶׁר וְאִם־בֵּין כּוֹכָבִים שִׂים קִנֶּךָ
These two expressions have similar meanings. This is a way of showing that something is important by saying it more than once but in slightly different ways.
אִם־תַּגְבִּיהַּ כַּנֶּשֶׁר וְאִם־בֵּין כּוֹכָבִים שִׂים קִנֶּךָ

The people of Edom think that they are safe because they live up high in the mountains. The Lord is saying that even if they lived much higher than it is actually possible for humans to live, they would still not be safe.
Here, bring you down means “humble you” or “defeat you.” This is a spatial metaphor. The Lord’s response to the Edomites is that there is nowhere they would be safe from his judgment and punishment.
1:5: These two phrases mean the same thing. The repetition is used to emphasize the one idea that they are expressing.
This is a rhetorical question. The question form is used to make a point strongly.
אִם־בֹּצְרִים בָּאוּ לָךְ הֲלוֹא יַשְׁאִירוּ עֹלֵלוֹת
This is a rhetorical question. The question form is used to make a point strongly.
1:6: Here, the name Esau refers to the people of Edom. They were the descendants of Esau, who was also known as Edom. All the people of Edom are being portrayed as if they were a single person, their ancestor.
Here, ransacked means that the enemies have searched through the people’s things, taken everything valuable, and left everything else in a mess or damaged.
1:7: The Lord is still addressing the people of Edom here, so the word your refers to them.
Here, the border could mean: (1) It could refer to the border of the country of Edom; or (2) it could refer to the border of a formerly friendly country.
כֹּל אַנְשֵׁי בְרִיתֶךָ … אַנְשֵׁי שְׁלֹמֶךָ לַחְמְךָ
All three phrases refer to Edom’s allies. The Lord is showing that what he is saying is important by saying it more than once in similar ways.

This phrase could mean: (1) the Lord is saying this as an aside to express his evaluation of the people of Edom. (2) the former allies could be saying this about Edom; (3) It could be referring to the trap just mentioned; (4) It could be referring to the shocking situation of Edom being betrayed by its allies.
Here, him probably refers to Edom, which represents the people who live there.
1:8: הֲלוֹא בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא … וְהַאֲבַדְתִּי חֲכָמִים מֵאֱדוֹם
This is a rhetorical question. The Lord uses the question form here to emphasize that he will certainly do this.
The original audience would have known that Edom was famous for its wisdom. So this means that even their famous wisdom cannot save them from the Lord’s destruction.
This is the second part of the rhetorical question. The Lord continues the question form here to emphasize that he will certainly do this.
In this poetic style, the reader is expected to use the words will I not on that day destroy from the first rhetorical question in order to understand this second one.

In this poetic style, the same meaning is expressed twice but in different words in order to emphasize what is being said. Here, wise men and understanding both refer to people who are wise, and Edom and the mountain of Esau are both ways of referring to the country of Edom.
The Lord is referring to the whole territory of Edom by using the name of one prominent part of it. The mountain of Esau may be the one now called Mount Bozrah.
This is the name of the man who was the ancestor of the people of Edom.
1:9: The Lord continues speaking to the people of Edom, but now he addresses them as Teman, which was the name of the region around their capital city. This part of Edom is now being used to represent the whole people.
Teman is the name of a region in the land of Edom. The Lord is referring to the whole territory of Edom by the name of one part of it.
Here, cut off is a metaphor for being killed. The Edomites are pictured as part of the mountain where they live, and their death as being cut off from the mountain.
Here, a man is an idiom that means “each person.”
As in v. 8, the Lord is referring to the whole territory by the name of this one part of it.
1:10: The term brother is being used here to refer to members of a related people group.
Here the name Jacob refers to the people of Judah, who were his descendants. All the people are being portrayed as if they were a single person, their ancestor.
To be covered with something is an idiom for fully experiencing it.
As in 1:5, cut off is an idiom for being destroyed.
1:11: This is a metaphor that pictures the people of Edom as a person who was just standing around and not helping a relative.
שְׁבוֹת זָרִים חֵילוֹ וְנָכְרִים בָּאוּ שערו
These two phrases mean similar things. They are used together to emphasize that Judah was in a desperate situation. Invading armies were plundering the cities of Judah.
Here, his refers to your brother Jacob in 1:10, meaning the people of Judah.
In this context, the term translated wealth could also mean “army.” But since it clearly means “wealth” in 1:13, it seems best to translate it as “wealth” here, as well.
Here, gates stands for “city.” The gates, the part of a city through which people would come and go, are being used to represent the whole city.

There are two possibilities for what this could mean: (1) This is a figurative way of saying that the foreigners had complete control of Jerusalem, with Jerusalem pictured as something that everybody wants to have, but it cannot be divided, so they cast lots to see who will get it; or (2) The name of the city may be standing for the wealth of the city.
The people of Edom did not do exactly the same things as the strangers and foreigners did, but they were like them because they did not help the people of Judah, who were a related people group.
1:12: The Lord uses a repetitive series of sentences in verses 12–14 to show how badly the people of Edom have treated the people of Judah. This repetitive style of speaking or writing is called a “litany.” This is a list of the charges against the people of Edom. The Lord goes on to say in verses 15 and 16 that he has found them guilty of all of these charges and that he will punish them.
Here, on the day is an idiom that refers to an undefined period of time that could extend from one to very many days.
As in 1:10, the Lord describes the people of Judah as a brother to the descendants of Esau, because their ancestor, Jacob, was the brother of Esau (Edom).
This is an idiom for bragging or mocking. In this context of observing someone else’s misfortune, mocking makes better sense.
1:13: בְּיוֹם אֵידָם … בְּיוֹם אֵידוֹ … בְּיוֹם אֵידוֹ
In this poetic style, the same phrase is used at the end of each line to emphasize how terrible the calamity was.

In the first line of this verse, their refers to my people. In the second and third lines, God’s people are once again pictured as their ancestor Jacob, and so the singular pronoun his is used (See: 1:10).

Here, the word translated as you is feminine and plural. In the rest of Obadiah, it is masculine and singular. It may be that God is addressing the women specifically here in case they thought that they were not also guilty. So use a feminine plural form here, or mark this in some other way so that it means “you women.”
1:14: A crossroads is a place where two roads come together.
Here, to cut down is a metaphor that means “to kill.” It is likely a comparison to the way grain is cut down at harvest time.
1:15: Bible experts are not certain whether verse 15 goes with verse 14 as the end of the previous section or if it goes with verse 16 as the beginning of the new section. Many Bibles put a section break and a heading before verse 15, such as “God Will Judge the Nations.”

Here the Lord is giving the people of Edom the reason why they should not have done all of the bad things that they did to the Israelites that were listed in verses 11–14, and instead of that, helped them. It is because the Lord will soon judge all nations for the way that they have treated others.
The day of the Lord is an expression that refers to a specific time when God punishes people for their sins.
In this context, near means “close in time.”
This is a metaphor that pictures the Edomites as having sent bad things out to others, and now those things are going to come back and hurt them as they land on their heads.
The head is being used to represent the whole person.
1:16: As at the beginning of verse 15, here also the connecting word For indicates that this is a reason why the people of Edom should have helped the Israelites instead of joining in attacking them. Here also the Lord describes how he will soon judge all nations for the way that they have treated others. Choosing between these possibilities depends on how you interpret the referent of the word you. The word you here is masculine plural, the first and only time it occurs in this form in the book. Throughout the book, the nation of Edom was addressed with the masculine singular form. This is also the last occurrence of the second person in the book. (1) Because of these observations, the use of drinking here and throughout the Bible as a metaphor for suffering punishment, and the location of this suffering on Mount Zion in Jerusalem, it seems that here Obadiah stops addressing the people of Edom and returns to addressing the people of Israel. At the beginning of the book, Obadiah included the people of Israel when he said, “We have heard a report from the Lord.” Now, near the end of the book, he addresses them again, giving them assurance that the people of Edom will be punished for what they did to the people of Israel. (2) This word you could refer to the people of Edom.
The image of drinking something is often used in the Bible as a metaphor for suffering or for being punished by God.

The mountain of my holiness refers to Mount Zion and therefore to the city of Jerusalem. So here Jerusalem is being referred to by the name of something closely associated with it, the mountain that the city is built on.
Here the metaphor continues, using drink to mean “suffer” or “be punished.”
The words translated drink and swallow mean very similar things and are used together to intensify the one meaning.
Here the metaphor continues, using drink and swallow as images for suffering or being punished.
1:17: This is a figure of speech that refers to Jerusalem by the name of something closely associated with it, the mountain that the city is built on.
Here, the house of Jacob is an idiom that means “the descendants of Jacob” and by extension, all of the people of Israel.
Here, possessions refers to the land that was supposed to be passed down from generation to generation to each of the Israelite families and clans.
1:18: וְהָיָה בֵית־יַעֲקֹב אֵשׁ וּבֵית יוֹסֵף לֶהָבָה

These two expressions have similar meanings. The Lord is showing that what he is saying is important by saying it more than once. Both house of Jacob and house of Joseph stand for all of the Israelites.
Here, the word house means all of the people descended from a particular person. All of the descendants of Jacob are being described as if they were one household living together.

The descendants of Joseph are also being described as if they were one household. Joseph was the son of Jacob, and his descendants made up a large part of the people of Israel. So the Lord is using his descendants to represent the whole nation.
The descendants of Esau (Edom) are also being described as if they were one household.

In this metaphor, the Lord is saying that the Israelites will be like fire and flame, that the people of Edom will be like dry grass, and that the Israelites will do to the people of Edom what fire and flame do to dry grass. In other words, just as fire and flame burn up dry grass until it is all gone, the Israelites who survive will conquer all of Edom.
The word stubble means the dry pieces of plants that are left in the ground after their stalks have been cut.
Burn and consume mean almost the same thing. The Lord uses the words together to intensify the meaning.
Here, For indicates that what follows is the reason for what came before. The Lord is reminding the reader that these things will certainly happen, because this message comes from him.
1:19: This verse as a whole describes people who live in different parts of Israel conquering the territories next to them.

The Negev is the name of the southern region of Judea that is dry, rocky, and barren. It is being used to represent the people who live there. The people are being described by the name of something closely associated with them, the land that they live in.
This was one of the mountains in Edom. The Lord is referring to the whole territory of Edom by using the name of one prominent part of it.

The Shephelah is the name of the western foothills in the land of Israel. That location is being used to represent the people who live there. The people are being described by the name of something closely associated with them, the land that they live in.
The Philistines were people who occupied the territory to the west of Israel. Here, the people are used to represent that territory, also known as the region of Phoenicia.
Here, field refers to a large, open area, and represents the whole territory that belonged to the tribe of Ephraim and that surrounded the city of Samaria.
Here, Benjamin represents the people of the tribe of Benjamin. All the people are being portrayed as if they were a single person, their ancestor.
Gilead is a region east of the land of Israel, across the Jordan River. It is being used to represent the areas to the east.
1:20: Here, the word translated as army can also mean “a large number of people.” In this context, the large number of people are also described as capturing territory, so they will be acting as an army. If not, then choose the term that fits best.

Here, there are two possibilities for the meaning of the sons of Israel: (1) In this context, Israel is identified as occupying territory in the north and is in contrast with Jerusalem, so it seems that the sons of Israel is referring to people who are from the northern kingdom of Israel; (2) It could refer to all of the descendants of Israel.
The land of Canaan is where the people of Israel lived before they were exiled. So the people are being called by the name of the place where they lived, and where they will live again.
Zarephath was a Phoenician city north of Israel on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea between Tyre and Sidon.

Sepharad is the name of a place whose location is unknown to modern scholars. Some experts suggest that it refers to the city of Sardis in the region of Lydia. This would be in Asia Minor, northwest of Israel, in what is now the country of Turkey.
In order to conquer the cities of the Negev, these exiles first will return from the distant lands where they are living.
The Negev is the name of the southern region of Judea that is dry, rocky, and barren.
1:21: וְעָלוּ מוֹשִׁעִים בְּהַר צִיּוֹן לִשְׁפֹּט אֶת־הַר עֵשָׂו

Even though the mountain of Zion is a figurative name for Jerusalem, it would be good to keep the imagery of this high place in Jerusalem where God’s temple was, if possible. This would also allow the comparison with the mountain of Esau. Edom had boasted that it was up high and that no one could bring it down.
Here, saviors refers to Israelite military leaders whom God will use to defeat the nation of Edom.
The Lord is referring to Jerusalem by the name of something closely associated with it, the mountain that the city is built on.
This phrase refers to the mountainous territory where Esau, the brother of Jacob and the ancestor of the Edomites, went and settled.
This phrase emphasizes that the Lord will personally rule over the kingdom of Israel as they rule over Edom.
